summary: Front mark of the Liston range on the Delaware River: a frame Colonial Revival house and light tower lit in 1908, now private, with a Coast Guard light still on a steel tower.

light.characteristic: Occulting white, 2 s on and 1 s dark, clockwork shutter (historic light, 1908-1932)

lens.where: lantern room of the house; not the original lens (nomination, 2003)

structures.type: frame light tower on a Colonial Revival frame dwelling

structures.material: masonry (white glazed brick oil house); frame garage

structures.type: harbor defense gun emplacement and magazine
white skeleton tower on a tank house, 40 ft in front of the dwelling
structures.note: The light moved to this tower. A steel electrified tower of the mid-1950s is still in use as an aid to navigation (nomination).

access.note: Private property within the Bayview Beach community; grounds, dwelling and tower closed (LighthouseFriends).

facts.agency: United States Coast Guard (the active light); private owner (the house)

events.note: Government bought about five acres from Sarah R. Burbridge on 18 June 1903 for $1,350
Temporary headlight lantern on a lantern post first lit 25 October 1904
Port Penn Front Range light discontinued and replaced by the Liston Range lights
Contract accepted 7 October 1907: low bid of $11,645 by Warner and Blair of Claymont
Permanent light first shown from the lantern room, 28 December 1908
390 feet of reinforced concrete wall built at the station
Five riprap jetties in timber cribs added to protect the wall's base
Fourth-order Fresnel lens installed (nomination). LighthouseFriends gives a Macbeth fourth-order range lens from the start; USLHS gives a second-order range lens in 1906.
Storm damage: earth cut away from the reservation; the 1924-1929 index calls it a hurricane
House and navigational aid electrified; kerosene lamp until 1932
Responsibility passed to the United States Coast Guard
Delaware National Guard coast artillery section set up guns at the station from 8 December 1941; concrete emplacements finished by May 1942; abandoned December 1942
Keeper Harry E. Spencer died at the station (LighthouseFriends; nomination says early 1940s)
House closed, according to the nomination; LighthouseFriends gives 1948 as the date Sophia Spencer left
Light moved to a white skeleton tower 40 ft in front of the house
House and most of the property declared in excess and put up for sale (nomination)
Sold at public auction for $8,200 (LighthouseFriends); sale date differs from the nomination's 1953
Sold to a private owner (name withheld in this research file)
Listed on the National Register in January 2004 (LighthouseFriends)

corrections.why: The permanent light was first shown on 28 December 1908 (nomination; LighthouseFriends; Delaware Bay keepers' group). The 1906 date is the USLHS 'Year Established' and the temporary light was lit in October 1904.

corrections.proposed: frame house and frame light tower, built 1908; the skeletal and steel towers are later (1952 and mid-1950s)
corrections.why: The 1907-08 house and tower are wood frame (nomination). The iron or steel towers belong to the Coast Guard's later light.

corrections.proposed: no event for this station; the 1877 date belongs to the Port Penn range
corrections.why: The nomination dates the house to 1907-08 and the lights to the 1904 temporary light; the USLHS 1877 tower entry does not match the frame tower described in the nomination.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1953 figure matches the 1952 skeleton tower and the 1953 sale in the nomination; the house itself was first shown in December 1908.

notes_for_editor: (1) Lens: the nomination gives a fourth-order Fresnel lens installed 1916 and a fourth-order lens now in the lantern room that is not the original; LighthouseFriends gives a Macbeth fourth-order range lens from the start; the USLHS record gives a second-order range lens installed 1906. The record's 'order 2, in_place' is not supported by the nomination, which reports a fourth-order lens. Not corrected here. (2) Historic characteristic: occulting 2 s on and 1 s dark (nomination; Delaware Bay keepers' group); the record's 'Iso W 6s' is unverified and was not changed. The current Coast Guard characteristic and focal height were not read from the Light List. (3) Focal height: record 13.7 m; USLHS '36 feet above water'; Delaware Bay keepers' group '50 feet above mean high water'. Not used. (4) Range: the record's 15.0 nm is not the figure the nomination gives; the nomination's 17.5 nm is for the whole range. (5) Keeper dates: the roster gives Duncan 1904-1906, but the nomination says he never lived in the house and moved to New Castle Rear in January 1909. The roster starts Spencer in 1928; the nomination and LighthouseFriends say 1927. The rear story in staging batch h3 gives Spencer as head keeper at the rear 1913-1928, while the nomination calls him assistant keeper at the rear before 1927; the rear's checker should look at this. (6) Dates for closing and sale: house closed 1950 (nomination) vs keeper left 1948 (LighthouseFriends); the skeleton tower went up in 1952 (nomination) and a mid-1950s steel tower is described as still in use; the sale was 1953 (nomination) or public auction in 1954 (LighthouseFriends). (7) Port Penn Front: the nomination says erected 1875 and operated from 1871; LighthouseFriends says the range was established 1877. Not resolved; relevant to the Port Penn station. (8) The USLHS record's tower data (wrought iron, 1877, pyramidal skeletal, 36 ft) do not match the frame tower in the nomination; flagged for a human check. (9) Private owners are not named. The nomination's author is the owner; LighthouseFriends names the owners and the 1953-54 buyer. These names are left out under the rule on living private residents. The Spencer family account is second-hand, from LighthouseFriends. (10) Newspaper searches for the 1908 first light and the 1953 sale timed out (Chronicling America rate limit) and produced no source. (11) No wreck or rescue tied to the front light was found in the sources read. (12) Commissioner's report tables for 1915-1916 list 'Listons Range Front' with figures (for example 1,460) whose meaning is not clear; not used. (13) USLHS roster lists Sophia Spencer under principal keeper; role set to lamplighter per the nomination and LighthouseFriends. (14) Corpus Lighthouse Board volumes for 1904-1910 are not in the local corpus; the 1904 and 1908 dates rest on the nomination and LighthouseFriends. (15) A second record, us-de-liston-range-front-2 (39.762, -75.561), exists in data/stations/de and may be a duplicate or a mislocated record; not used here. (16) No photos were added. (17) The nomination dates the Lighthouse Service's move to the Department of Commerce to 1890 and the Coast Guard transfer to 1939. The story attributes both to the nomination. The 1890 date is flagged for a human check: the Department of Commerce and Labor was created in 1903, and the lighthouse establishment moved to it then, so the nomination's date may be wrong. (18) The 1928 storm: the 1928 bulletin describes a severe tropical storm with warnings from 18 September; the Liston damage is in the same report, so the story dates it to September 1928. (19) Sophia Spencer is listed by the roster as a principal keeper; the nomination and LighthouseFriends call her a lamplighter, and the story states both. (20) The 1904 Port Penn discontinuance is dated 1877 for the range by LighthouseFriends and 1875 for the station by the nomination; not used in the story.
